units.title: Unit 39 — Running a company
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 84–85 (PDF pages 85–86).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition)
units.category: Company organisation, management, growth and business relationships
learningObjectives: Discuss a company’s goals, achievements, employees, products, quality and customer demand.
Describe setting up, running, expanding and taking over a business, using appropriate verb patterns.
Recognise distinctions between a head office and a branch, and between a client and a customer.
Use currently, former and formerly accurately when discussing business history.
Talk about professional contacts, business expertise, publicity and ambitions.

items.example: The team achieved its goals earlier than expected.
items.note: Achieve means succeed at something that requires effort.

items.example: Opening a second shop was a major achievement.
items.note: Countable noun related to achieve.

items.pt: alcançar muitas conquistas; realizar muita coisa
items.example: This small company has achieved a great deal in five years.
items.note: A great deal means a lot, especially of success or progress.

items.example: The business has changed a great deal recently.
items.note: A formal-neutral alternative to a lot; used for amount or degree.

items.example: Her grandparents started the family business.
items.note: A business owned or operated by members of a family.

items.example: The bakery sells bread made early each morning.
items.note: A place where bread and cakes are made or sold.

items.example: Three generations of the family work together.
items.note: A group of people in a family born around a similar period.

items.example: The business currently employs eighty people.
items.note: Currently means now, not actually in the sense of in fact.

items.example: I thought the shop had closed, but it is actually still open.
items.note: Actually means in fact; it does not mean currently or at present.

items.example: Every employee receives regular safety training.
items.note: A person employed and paid by a company.

items.example: They set up a company to sell organic food.
items.note: Set up means establish a business; do not confuse with take up a hobby or role.

items.pt: abrir um negócio; fundar uma empresa
items.example: My sister plans to set up a business next year.
items.note: The separable verb set up means establish or start an organisation.

items.example: Our main aim is to reduce waste.
items.note: Here aim is a noun for something you hope to achieve.

items.pt: com o objetivo de; visando a
items.example: The firm opened another factory with the aim of increasing production.
items.note: Follow with the -ing form: with the aim of improving, not improve.

items.example: Customers enjoy the variety of products in this shop.
items.note: Variety indicates different kinds of things.

items.example: The café offers a variety of fresh sandwiches.
items.note: A variety of is followed by a plural countable noun or a mass noun.

items.example: The company checks the quality of every product.
items.note: How good or bad a product or service is.

items.example: They use local ingredients of the highest quality.
items.note: The highest quality describes the best standard.

items.example: Demand for fresh bread increases at weekends.
items.note: Demand for something means how much customers want it.

items.example: There is growing demand for products without plastic packaging.
items.note: Growing describes demand that is increasing.

items.example: The market has a separate section for organic products.
items.note: Organic refers to food produced using specified agricultural methods.

items.example: She's an expert in food safety.
items.note: Expert can be a countable noun or an adjective.

items.example: He's an expert in international finance.
items.note: Use expert in or on for fields of specialist knowledge; the exercise uses in.

items.example: She runs a company with thirty staff members.
items.note: Run means manage or control operations, not move on foot.

items.pt: administrar um negócio; gerir uma empresa
items.example: His brother runs the business from a small office.
items.note: A common way to describe managing a company.

items.example: The shop receives daily deliveries.
items.note: Daily can be an adjective or adverb meaning every day.

items.example: They deliver bread to restaurants each morning.
items.note: Deliver goods to a place or recipient.

items.example: Your delivery will arrive before noon.
items.note: Related noun to deliver; a helpful family extension.

items.example: She joined a small engineering firm.
items.note: Firm is a business noun, often for professional services.

items.example: The company hopes to expand into new regions.
items.note: A business expands when it becomes bigger.

items.example: The delivery service expanded rapidly after its first year.
items.note: Exercise context uses rapid business growth.

items.example: The expansion created several new jobs.
items.note: A useful noun from expand; not a separate source-page headword.

items.example: An accountant checks the firm's financial records.
items.note: Professional who prepares or checks financial information.

items.example: She works for a firm of accountants in Leeds.
items.note: A professional-services company made up of accountants.

items.example: The former director now works abroad.
items.note: Former describes a previous role or title, not a current one.

items.example: A former owner of the shop returned for its anniversary.
items.note: A previous owner; the present owner may be someone else.

items.example: The company was formerly known as Valley Foods.
items.note: Adverb meaning in the past, but not now.

items.example: He still shares a business with his ex-wife.
items.note: Use ex- especially for former personal relationships, such as ex-wife.

items.pt: assumir o controle de uma empresa; adquirir uma empresa
items.example: A larger group took over the company last year.
items.note: Take over means gain control of a business; unlike setting it up.

items.pt: ser adquirido; passar ao controle de outra empresa
items.example: The local business was taken over by a national chain.
items.note: Passive construction of take over in the business-acquisition sense.

items.pt: assumir um cargo; começar a exercer uma função
items.example: She will take up a new position in September.
items.note: Take up a position means start working in a role.

items.example: My manager took up tennis during his holiday.
items.note: Take up means start a hobby or activity, not establish a company.

items.example: The senior partner is responsible for the largest clients.
items.note: A senior partner is an experienced or leading partner in a firm.

items.example: The company's headquarters are in Manchester.
items.note: Headquarters refers to the main offices; it takes singular or plural agreement depending on usage.

items.example: The bank opened a new branch in Bristol.
items.note: Here branch is one office of a larger company; not a tree branch.

items.example: She has business contacts across the country.
items.note: Contacts are people you know who may be useful professionally.

items.example: The lawyer called her client to discuss the contract.
items.note: Professional advisers such as lawyers and accountants have clients.

items.pt: cliente; comprador de loja ou negócio
items.example: The customer paid for the shoes at the till.
items.note: Shops and retailers generally have customers rather than clients.

items.example: The unusual advert attracted attention online.
items.note: A common collocation for becoming noticed.

items.example: The firm decided to advertise on local radio.
items.note: To promote products or services publicly.

items.example: Her ambition is to lead an international team.
items.note: An important personal goal that someone wants to achieve.

items.example: He has the ambition to open a second branch.
items.note: The infinitive follows ambition to when expressing an intended action.

items.pt: imagem pública; percepção que as pessoas têm
items.example: The company worked hard to improve its public image.
items.note: Here image means reputation or public perception, not a photograph.

items.example: The company has offices in three cities.
items.note: An organisation that sells goods or services.

items.pt: ter contatos em; conhecer pessoas de um setor
items.example: I have contacts in banking who may be able to help.
items.note: In names the professional field or industry.

items.example: The firm achieved success through careful planning.
items.note: Natural collocation reinforcing achieve and business success.

sectionsChecked: A · A successful business: achievements, family-business bakery profile, workforce, growth and operational verbs
A · Language help: achieve vs achievement; currently not actually
B · A view of a company: accountants, takeover, senior partner, headquarters, branches, clients and publicity
B · Language help: former vs ex, client vs customer, set up vs take up
Exercises 39.1–39.5: people, definitions, semantic contrasts, paraphrases, business profile

units.title: Unit 40 — Business and finance
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 86–87 (PDF pages 87–88).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition)
units.category: Financial concepts, company performance and trend language
learningObjectives: Describe upward, downward and unchanged trends and their speed with precise adverbs.
Use rise, fall, increase and decrease with the correct prepositions and distinguish rise from raise.
Explain profit, loss, price, sales, value, loans, interest and interest rates in clear English.
Discuss inflation, trade, recession, currencies and economic indicators.
Read a simple sales chart using figures, units sold, quarters and time expressions.

items.pt: tendência; movimento ao longo do tempo
items.example: The graph shows a clear upward trend in sales.
items.note: A trend is the general direction in which something changes over time.

items.example: Sales improved after the company reduced its prices.
items.note: Can refer to the quantity or value of goods sold.

items.example: Fuel prices may rise next month.
items.note: Rise is intransitive: prices rise; someone raises prices.

items.example: The cost of electricity went up in April.
items.note: Everyday alternative to rise or increase.

items.example: Demand increased after the advertisement appeared.
items.note: As a verb increase commonly has stress on the second syllable.

items.example: There was an increase in orders last week.
items.note: The noun often stresses the first syllable and is followed by in or of.

items.example: The price rose slightly in January.
items.note: Slightly describes a small change.

items.example: Sales rose gradually during the summer.
items.note: Gradually describes a slow change over time.

items.example: The cost of materials rose sharply last year.
items.note: Sharply describes a fast or large increase.

items.example: Profits were slightly higher this quarter.
items.note: Adverb describing a small amount of difference.

items.example: Production gradually returned to normal.
items.note: Adverb meaning slowly over a period of time.

items.example: Prices fell sharply after the announcement.
items.note: Adverb meaning suddenly or by a large amount in trend descriptions.

items.example: The number of visitors fell during winter.
items.note: Fall is an intransitive verb in trend language; past tense fell.

items.example: The price of tickets went down on Monday.
items.note: Everyday opposite of go up.

items.example: Demand decreased during the recession.
items.note: Verb often stresses the second syllable; can be intransitive or transitive.

items.example: There was a decrease in customer complaints.
items.note: Noun commonly stressed on the first syllable.

items.example: Ticket sales fell sharply after the price rise.
items.note: Describes a sudden or large downward change.

items.example: Our monthly rent stayed the same this year.
items.note: No increase or decrease; the amount is unchanged.

items.example: The number of orders rose by ten per cent.
items.note: Use by to express the size of a change, rather than the final value.

items.example: The number of complaints fell from eighty to fifty.
items.note: From marks the starting value and to the final value.

items.pt: uma alta nos preços; aumento de preços
items.example: A rise in prices affected many families.
items.note: Rise in identifies the thing that increased.

items.example: An increase in profit allowed the firm to hire more workers.
items.note: Use increase in to identify the measure that changed.

items.word: a decrease of ten per cent
items.pt: uma diminuição de dez por cento
items.example: The accounts showed a decrease of ten per cent.
items.note: Decrease of names the amount or percentage of the change.

items.example: There was a sharp fall in sales in February.
items.note: Sharp is an adjective modifying the noun fall.

items.example: The supplier plans to raise prices in July.
items.note: Raise requires an object: a company raises prices, whereas prices rise.

items.example: The company reported a higher profit this year.
items.note: Money left after a business has paid its costs; opposite loss.

items.example: The restaurant began to make a profit after six months.
items.note: The usual verb is make, not do, a profit.

items.example: The business recorded a loss in its first year.
items.note: In business, a loss occurs when costs exceed earnings.

items.example: The firm made a loss when orders fell.
items.note: The opposite of make a profit.

items.example: A healthy economy supports new jobs.
items.note: A country's system of money, trade, work and production.

items.pt: a economia melhora; a atividade econômica se recupera
items.example: The economy improves when more businesses invest and hire.
items.note: Improve describes a positive change; not a guarantee of growth in every sector.

items.example: The rise in orders is a positive sign for the factory.
items.note: Evidence that a development may be improving.

items.example: She applied for a bank loan to buy equipment.
items.note: Money borrowed that is normally paid back.

items.example: The company used a bank loan to open another shop.
items.note: A sum borrowed from a bank.

items.pt: contratar um empréstimo; pegar um empréstimo
items.example: They took out a loan to buy a new machine.
items.note: Common expression for arranging to borrow from a lender.

items.example: We had to borrow money to repair the roof.
items.note: Borrow means receive money that must be returned; lend is the opposite perspective.

items.example: The bank charges interest on the loan.
items.note: Interest is the extra amount paid for borrowing; not interest meaning curiosity.

items.example: The interest rate is fixed for the first year.
items.note: The percentage used to calculate interest.

items.example: Some lenders charge higher interest on short loans.
items.note: Charge interest means require a borrower to pay extra money.

items.example: I will pay back the money over twelve months.
items.note: A separable phrasal verb: pay it back, not pay back it.

items.example: High inflation makes everyday goods more expensive.
items.note: The rate at which the general level of prices increases.

items.pt: temores crescentes; preocupações cada vez maiores
items.example: There are growing fears of another rise in prices.
items.note: Means increasing worry about a possible negative development.

items.word: rise by as much as two per cent
items.pt: aumentar em até dois por cento; subir até dois por cento
items.example: The charge could rise by as much as two per cent.
items.note: As much as introduces an upper-limit estimate of the change; two per cent is a model amount.

items.example: The bank offered an interest rate of five per cent.
items.note: British spelling uses two words; 5% is read five per cent.

items.example: The latest figures show that sales are recovering.
items.note: Figures means numerical information, not illustrated shapes.

items.example: Trade between the two countries increased last year.
items.note: Buying and selling goods or services, especially internationally.

items.example: Production grew for four months in a row.
items.note: Means consecutively, with no break.

items.example: The value of the pound changed during the week.
items.note: What an asset or currency is worth.

items.example: The euro is the currency used in several countries.
items.note: Money officially used in a country or monetary area.

items.pt: em relação ao dólar; frente ao dólar
items.example: The pound rose against the dollar today.
items.note: Against indicates a currency exchange comparison.

items.example: The company's sales were strong in the final quarter.
items.note: In business, one quarter is a period of three months.

items.pt: aumentar as expectativas positivas; alimentar esperanças
items.example: Better sales figures raised hopes of a recovery.
items.note: Raise is transitive; its object is hopes.

items.example: Several shops closed during the recession.
items.note: A period when overall economic activity is weak or falling.

items.pt: sair da recessão; começar a recuperar-se
items.example: The country may come out of recession next year.
items.note: An expression for a possible return to economic growth after recession.

items.pt: unidades vendidas; quantidade de produtos vendidos
items.example: The graph compares the number of units sold each year.
items.note: Used as a chart-axis label for the quantity sold.

items.pt: dados de vendas; números de vendas
items.example: The sales figures were higher in the second quarter.
items.note: The numerical quantities or values recorded for sales.

items.example: The graph shows three years of sales data.
items.note: A diagram representing numerical information visually.

items.example: A sharp decrease in orders followed the price increase.
items.note: Sharp means sudden or large in descriptions of change.

items.example: There was a rise in price after the shop changed its supplier.
items.note: Rise is a noun for an increase; a seller can raise a price.

B · Financial language: four short reports, international trade chart and economic vocabulary
B · Language help: interest, interest rate, borrowing and paying back
Exercises 40.1–40.5: prepositions, definitions, loan calculations, illustrated sales graph and discussion
